extracted.intended_audience: federal agencies (rule writers), eRulemaking project offices, and members of the public who submit rulemaking comments
extracted.subtask_description: Best-practices guidance for agencies and the eRulemaking Project Management Office on (1) how to solicit, accept, post, and manage public comments and (2) what practices will produce useful, participatory, and reliable comment records for notice-and-comment rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish guidance explaining what comments are most beneficial
rubrics_metrics.description: The eRulemaking Project Management Office should consider publishing a document explaining what types of comments are most beneficial and listing best practices for parties submitting comments. Individual agencies may publish supplements to the common document describing the qualities of effective comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once developed, these documents should be made publicly available by posting on the agency website, Regulations.gov, and any other venue that will promote widespread availability of the information. (Recommendation 1)

rubrics_metrics.name: Set comment periods to promote participation while ensuring efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should set comment periods that consider the competing interests of promoting optimal public participation while ensuring that the rulemaking is conducted efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a general matter, for "significant regulatory actions" as defined in Executive Order 12,866 (as supplemented by Exec. Order 13,563), agencies should use a comment period of at least 60 days. For all other rulemakings, they should generally use a comment period of at least 30 days. When agencies set shorter comment periods in appropriate circumstances, they are encouraged to provide an appropriate explanation for doing so. (Recommendation 2; cites Exec. Order No. 13,563 and prior ACUS Recommendation 93-4.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt stated policies to post public comments online promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt stated policies of posting public comments to the Internet within a specified period after submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should post all electronically submitted comments on the Internet and should scan and post comments submitted in paper format. The recommendation cites OIRA guidance expecting timely posting of public comments to electronic dockets (Regulations.gov), regardless of submission method. (Recommendation 3)

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish and publish policies on anonymous comment submission
rubrics_metrics.description: The eRulemaking Project Management Office and individual agencies should establish and publish policies regarding the submission of anonymous comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should decide and make public their positions on confidentiality and anonymity of comments so prospective commenters know whether anonymous or confidential submissions will be accepted and under what terms. (Recommendation 4)

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt and publish consistent late-comment policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt and publish policies on late comments and should apply those policies consistently within each rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should determine whether they will accept late submissions in a given rulemaking and should announce the policy in publicly accessible forums (e.g., agency website, Regulations.gov) and in individual Federal Register notices requesting comments. The agency may state that late comments are disfavored and will only be considered to the extent practicable. Example provided: Federal Register notices sometimes state late comments will be included in the docket and considered as practicable. (Recommendation 5)

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reply-comment periods or other means for input on submitted comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate, agencies should make use of reply comment periods or other opportunities for receiving public input on submitted comments after all comments have been posted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opportunities for public input on submitted comments can include a reply period for written comments on submitted comments, an oral hearing, or some other means for input on comments received. The recommendation cites prior ACUS recommendations supporting second comment periods where comments raise new issues or conflicts of data, and OIRA memoranda encouraging such practices. (Recommendation 6)

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor dockets and refresh records when circumstances materially change
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should closely monitor their rulemaking dockets and, where a change in circumstances warrants it, consider using mechanisms such as supplemental notices of proposed rulemaking to refresh records that have become stale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should not automatically be deemed to "expire" after a fixed period, but agencies should use available mechanisms (e.g., supplemental NPRMs) when the agency believes circumstances have materially changed or the record has become stale. (Recommendation 7)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose the number of comments received in statement of basis and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should include in their statement of basis and purpose in the Federal Register, to the extent practicable, the number of comments received, or the number of commenters, in a rulemaking proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including the number of comments or commenters helps transparency about the extent of public participation in the proceeding. (Recommendation 8)
